author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the four chambers of the heart and their anatomical positions
Describe the four cardiac valves and their locations within the heart
Recognize the major blood vessels entering and leaving the heart
Trace the path of deoxygenated and oxygenated blood through the heart and lungs
Explain the structural and functional differences between the left and right ventricles
Understand how cardiac valves prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle

modules.description: Introduction to the four chambers of the heart, their relative sizes, and basic anatomical positioning. Students learn to identify the right and left atria and ventricles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the four chambers of the heart by location and name
Describe the relative wall thickness of each chamber
Explain the functional difference between atria and ventricles
Recognize why the left ventricle is thicker than the right ventricle
instructions: Observe the 3D heart model as it is rotated to show all four chambers
Listen to the narrator explain each chamber's location and function
Notice the difference in myocardial wall thickness between the right and left ventricles

clips.changeMeaning: Introduced the heart model rotating to display all four chambers from different angles, establishing the baseline anatomy.
clips.narration: The human heart is a muscular, four-chambered organ responsible for pumping blood throughout the body. The four chambers are the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle. The atria receive blood, while the ventricles pump blood out of the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: Labels for right atrium and left ventricle are now visible, helping students locate and identify key chambers. These will remain visible to anchor the viewer's attention.
clips.narration: Notice the positions: the right chambers are on the right side of the heart, and the left chambers are on the left. Both atria sit atop the ventricles. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps blood throughout the body.

clips.changeMeaning: The thickness indicator appears to visually emphasize the dramatic difference in myocardial wall thickness between the left and right ventricles. This directly addresses why structure matches function in cardiac anatomy.
clips.narration: Observe the wall thickness of the left ventricle—it is substantially thicker than the right ventricle. This is because the left ventricle must generate enough force to pump blood throughout the entire body via the systemic circulation. The right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs, so it requires less muscular force and a thinner wall.

modules.moduleName: Heart Valves and Blood Vessel Connections
modules.description: Students learn the locations and names of the four cardiac valves and the six major blood vessels that connect to the heart. This module establishes the pathways for blood flow in the next module.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the four cardiac valves by name and location
Name the six major blood vessels connected to the heart
Explain the function of each valve in preventing backflow
Describe the gross anatomy of the cardiac inlet and outlet pathways
instructions: Examine the heart model with valve labels positioned at their anatomical locations
Note the color-coding of vessels: deoxygenated blood in dark red, oxygenated blood in bright red
Observe how each valve is positioned between the chambers and vessels it controls

clips.changeMeaning: The heart model is repositioned at a 45-degree angle to better show valve locations. The first two valve labels (tricuspid and mitral) appear to establish the atrioventricular valve class.
clips.narration: The heart contains four valves that control the direction of blood flow and prevent backflow. Each valve is strategically positioned between two chambers or between a chamber and a vessel. The valves are the tricuspid valve, pulmonary valve, mitral valve, and aortic valve.

clips.changeMeaning: The six major blood vessels are now visible in the scene. Dark red coloring indicates deoxygenated vessels (vena cava, pulmonary arteries initially), while bright red indicates oxygenated vessels (aorta, pulmonary veins after lungs). This color-coding helps students distinguish blood oxygen status.
clips.narration: Six major blood vessels connect to the heart. The superior and inferior vena cava bring deoxygenated blood from the upper and lower body into the right atrium. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Finally, the aorta exits the left ventricle and distributes oxygenated blood to the entire body.

modules.moduleName: Blood Flow Through the Heart and Dual-Loop Circulation
modules.description: Students trace the complete pathway of blood through the heart across two full circuits: systemic circulation (body to heart to lungs pathway) and pulmonary circulation (lungs to heart to body pathway). This module animates blood flow and explains why structural asymmetry exists.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the path of deoxygenated blood from the body through the heart to the lungs
Trace the path of oxygenated blood from the lungs through the heart to the body
Explain the dual-loop circulation driven by the heart
Understand why the left ventricle requires greater muscle mass than the right ventricle
Describe the role of valves in maintaining unidirectional flow during the cardiac cycle
instructions: Watch as a blood particle traces through the right side of the heart to the lungs and back
Observe the second animation showing the left side of the heart pumping to the body
Note how valve closures prevent backflow at critical points in the cycle

components.text:
Left ventricle wall = 3x thicker
(Pumps entire body)

clips.changeMeaning: The lungs and a blood particle indicator appear. The text annotation highlights the right-side pathway. This establishes the first loop of dual circulation where the right heart specializes in pumping to the nearby lungs.
clips.narration: Let's trace the path of deoxygenated blood. Blood returns from the body through the superior and inferior vena cava into the right atrium. The right atrium contracts, pushing blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle then contracts, pushing blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries, which carry it to the lungs for oxygenation.

clips.changeMeaning: The systemic circulation representation and the left-side flow annotation appear. This highlights the second loop where the left heart, with its thicker myocardial wall, powers circulation throughout the entire body.
clips.narration: In the lungs, blood is oxygenated and returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The left atrium contracts, forcing blood through the mitral—or bicuspid—valve into the left ventricle. The left ventricle, with its thick muscular wall, then contracts powerfully and forces blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, which distributes oxygenated blood to the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: The ventricle thickness comparison text appears, directly connecting the structural observation from Module 1 to its functional purpose revealed in this module. This reinforces the principle that structure and function are intimately linked in anatomy.
clips.narration: Now you can see why structure matches function. The left ventricle has a wall three times thicker than the right ventricle because it must generate the force needed to pump blood through the entire systemic circulation—all the way to the extremities and back. The right ventricle only pumps blood a short distance to the lungs, so a thinner wall is sufficient. This structural asymmetry is a perfect example of how anatomy serves physiology.

clips.changeMeaning: All flow annotations and anatomical representations remain visible, allowing students to visualize how valve closure points create the one-way directional flow that makes the dual-loop circulation system efficient. This concludes the integrated view of structure enabling function.
clips.narration: The four valves prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle. When the atria contract, the atrioventricular valves—the tricuspid and mitral—open to allow blood into the ventricles. When the ventricles contract, these valves snap shut, preventing blood from flowing back into the atria. Similarly, the semilunar valves—the pulmonary and aortic—open when the ventricles contract but close immediately as they relax, preventing blood in the arteries from flowing backward into the ventricles. This one-way flow is essential for efficient circulation.
